blocks.text: A3 Benchmark cases
Six comparators were drawn from a 30-destination screen on twelve criteria, and each case reduces to a system type, two levers and the changes they require of the Western Cape.
Evaluation criteria

Both the Inception Report and the Global Benchmarking Report screen destinations on twelve criteria in four groups (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p29, p30; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p11). Each destination received one average score across all criteria (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p29).

blocks.caption: Benchmark selection criteria
blocks.source: Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p11 (groups, criteria and definitions, shortened); Inception Report, Nov 2025, p29, p30. Two inception criteria differ in definition as well as name (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p30). Cruise & Multi-Modal Access covers cruise arrivals, self-drive touring and regional mobility where the later report has Ease of Access & Visa. Tourism Infrastructure & Capacity covers hotel mix, transport, visitor services and attraction capacity where it has Airport & Tourism Infrastructure. Neither report prints scores by criterion, so the effect of the change on the ranking cannot be checked (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p31; Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p12).

blocks.text: The screen and how the set moved

The Inception Report described its starting universe as "an expansive list of 25+ destinations" and then scored 30 (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p29, p31). Its plan asked for "4 success cases and 2 that underperformed" (p16).

The Global Benchmarking Report also cites a screen of 30, keeps four of the inception six and presents no case as an underperformer (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p6, p12, p13). It drops Porto and Vancouver and adds Kenya and Auckland (p12), which ranked 11 and 7 in the inception screen (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p31). Three destinations scored 3.58, above Kenya's 3.50, and stayed out (p31). Neither document records why Porto and Vancouver were dropped.

blocks.text: Growth record and primary levers

The Global Benchmarking Report summarises the six cases in one table, reproduced here (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p9). Its global norm is growth of 3% to 5% a year under stable conditions (p7).

blocks.source: Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p9, values and destination labels as printed. Ranges are written with 'to', decimal commas are shown as points and Valencia's second lever takes its p49 title in place of the p9 label. Melbourne's ~4.3% is a forecast average annual growth rate for short-term visitor arrivals to Australia, not a 2023 to 2024 actual (p17). blocks.message: Five of the six printed growth rates exceed the report's 3% to 5% norm, two clearly beat 2024's actual global growth of 11%, and four of the six cases pair structural demand creation with demand activation.

blocks.text: System type and its three components

The report treats sustained growth as the product of three reinforcing components: institutional coordination; strategic marketing and promotion; accessibility and connectivity (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p58). Without competitive access, "latent demand does not convert" (p59).

All six cases align coordination, marketing and access, but each builds its system around a different anchor (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p61 for the system types; p59 to p60 for the three components, condensed).

**Melbourne and Victoria: events-led.** Coordination institutionalises events and a knowledge-led brand as a cross-government economic development tool. Marketing integrates city branding, intellectual capital and events into a single demand proposition. The event calendar is used to de-risk and stimulate aviation demand.

**Chile: connectivity-led.** Coordination is anchored around a single strategic constraint, long-haul access. Marketing runs unified national branding with defined regional identities and multi-region itinerary packaging. Liberal aviation policy and major hub investment position Santiago as a single efficient long-haul hub.

**Kenya: product-led.** Coordination aligns tourism with national priorities in conservation, trade and diplomacy. Marketing is segment-specific and grounded in a designed product system. Access reduces entry friction, with Nairobi as a multipurpose regional and global hub.

**Singapore: orchestrated experience.** A centrally orchestrated system under STB works through structured public-private partnerships. Marketing packages experiences (events, precincts, lifestyle) into seamless high-value propositions. Aviation, infrastructure and visitor experience are integrated into a single seamless gateway.

**Valencia: governance-led.** Governance is decentralised and sector-led. Marketing expands the reasons to visit: gastronomy, culture, sport, wellness and business events. Connectivity supports a multi-product destination system and dispersal.

**New Zealand: value-led.** Tourism, aviation and policy are integrated around shared demand objectives. Marketing shifts from volume to value by selling scarce, high-quality experiences. Long-haul demand converts only when marketing, aviation and distribution are aligned.
Levers and required changes

Each case closes on a transferable-levers slide that names two levers and the change each requires locally (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p13). The table gives those bullets in the report's words, shortened only by cutting.

blocks.caption: Transferable levers by case
blocks.source: Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p20 (Melbourne and Victoria), p28 (Chile), p35 (Kenya), p42 (Singapore), p49 (Valencia), p56 (New Zealand). Lever titles and bullets as printed, shortened by cutting, with one verb paraphrased; initial capitals, dashes and list commas follow this report's style.

columns.header: Lever 1 and required change for the Western Cape
Lever 2 and required change for the Western Cape

rows:
**Event Led Demand Engine**
Proactive international bidding pipeline anchored in priority markets and sectors; unified event acquisition and calendar strategy across Wesgro, Convention Bureau, City and Province; integrate city branding, intellectual capital and sector strengths into event positioning; hotel and precinct readiness planning; activate community participation and cultural engagement

**Knowledge-Led Brand Strategy**
Strengthen coordination between Wesgro and Convention Bureau/Universities/Industry Bodies/Trade and Investment Teams; proactive international conference bidding pipeline aligned to sector strengths; sector aligned brand narrative link to priority industries; visibility and packaging across global distribution channels

**Gateway-Led Air Connectivity and Capacity Expansion**
Treat air access as core economic infrastructure, not a tourism add-on; establish a permanent, well-funded Public-Private Air Access Fund; lobby for air service liberalisation and simplified visa regimes; develop a unified Gateway Narrative

**Product Diversification and Immersive Regional Positioning**
Unify destination narrative across province, city and sectors; move from asset marketing to experience led packaging; enforce brand consistency and international quality standards

**Wildlife-led Product Systematisation**
Shift from asset-led to system-led tourism development; strengthen coordination across public & private sector and communities; position WC as a demand anchor; integrate MICE and business travel into broader tourism system; build conservation and community inclusion into the tourism value proposition

**Nairobi-Led Gateway Repositioning and Demand Diversification**
Treat MICE as a system lever; align city, provincial and national actors around gateway strategy; infrastructure credibility and event-readiness must be protected; mitigate risk of MICE demand remaining disconnected

**Integrated Aviation Hub Strategy and Stopover Demand Conversion**
Align government, aviation, events and private sector stakeholders under a coordinated strategy with shared KPIs; linking air access, major events and co-op marketing to convert connectivity into high-value demand

**Institutional Quality Uplift of the Visitor Economy**
Province-wide quality and standards framework led by Wesgro; targeted investment in service excellence, work-force capability and infrastructure; embed continuous performance measurement and public-private accountability

**Integrated Quality & Sustainability Institutionalisation**
Establish a provincial-level quality authority or charter; phase implementation by district but embed in provincial policy; reduce SMME burden via subsidies and capability support; make certification visible across booking platforms; move from 'encouraged compliance' to institutionalised compliance

**Governance-led Demand Diversification**
Establish formal sector councils (Wine, MICE, Adventure, Culture etc.); embed tourism governance into permanent public-private structures; align infrastructure, promotion and policy by demand segment; integrate residents formally into planning forums

**Demand-Engineered Air Access**
Ring-fence budgets around priority long-haul corridors; formalise an Aviation Partnership Framework; introduce structured early-stage route support mechanisms

**Regional Value Engineering through Strategic De-Commoditisation**
Replace arrivals KPI with yield-based metrics; deliberate regional product curation frameworks; align conservation and premium access to protect pricing power; shape premium-ready regional circuits beyond Cape Town core; build partnerships with specialist distribution networks
blocks.message: The six cases yield twelve levers, and their required changes centre on air access, events, quality standards, regional product and governance.
